stem: A 76-year-old presents to the ED with 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea. He reports that he has not voided in the past 12 hours. His vitals are as follows: HR – 121, BP – 118/76, RR – 20, T – 37.1°C, O2 sat - 99% on room air. He looks unwell. His extremities are cool and cap refill is 4 seconds. Which of the following is TRUE?

options.html: This patient is not in shock because blood pressure is normal
Treatment is with IV D5W bolus
Provision of supplementary oxygen is critical
Treatment is with IV Ringer’s Lactate bolus

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). Shock is tissue hypoperfusion, not a blood pressure number: this man has tachycardia, cool extremities, cap refill 4 s and oliguria (no void in 12 h), and the lecture's class table keeps BP normal through class II losses, so A fails. The deficit is ECF volume from GI losses, so replace it with an isotonic crystalloid that stays in the ECF.

  • E: Ringer's lactate stays in the ECF (13 - IV Fluids, PoM 1 GU) - the right volume expander.
  • B: D5W is free water, distributing 2/3 into the ICF, so it barely expands plasma.
  • C: 0.5 mL/kg/h is the oliguria threshold / minimum resuscitation target rather than a 'normal' output (see flag).
  • D: sat is 99% on room air; oxygen is not the critical intervention here.

stem: A 22-year-old is brought to the ED after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. You assess for signs of tissue hypoperfusion. Which of the following would NOT be suggestive of shock?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). The lecture lists the eight features of shock: hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria, abnormal mental status, tachypnea, cool clammy cyanotic skin, metabolic acidosis and hyperlactatemia. A lactate of 1.1 sits inside the normal range, so it is the one finding that does not point to hypoperfusion (C).

  • A mottled skin - the cool, cyanotic skin of poor perfusion.
  • B altered mental status - brain hypoperfusion (anxious to confused through the classes).
  • D, E tachypnea and tachycardia - both on the list, and tachycardia is the first vital to move.

A normal lactate does not exclude early shock; it simply is not evidence for it.

stem: Which of the following are NOT part of the Hinshaw & Cox classification of shock?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The Hinshaw-Cox classification sorts shock by mechanism into four types: hypovolemic (low preload - hemorrhage, GI or renal losses), cardiogenic (pump failure - MI, arrhythmia, valve), obstructive (flow blocked outside the heart muscle - PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax) and distributive (vasodilation - sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic). 'Dissociative' is not a category of shock; the word belongs to psychiatry and anesthesia (ketamine), so A.

  • B, C, D, E: the four genuine categories.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.html: Hypotonic IV fluid administration results in water movement from the intracellular compartment to the extracellular compartment
D5 / 0.45% NS starts off as a hypertonic solution, but becomes hypotonic once dextrose is metabolized
Hypotonic IV fluids are a good choice for patients with elevated intracranial pressure
Hypertonic saline is primarily used to replace free water deficits

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 13 - IV Fluids (PoM 1 GU, Week 14). Dextrose is 'taken up into the body quickly, so the net effect is as if you gave free water'. D5/0.45% NS is therefore hypertonic in the bag (dextrose plus 77 mmol/L NaCl), but once the glucose is metabolized it is half-normal saline, which the lecture calls hypotonic. So B is true.

  • A: backwards - free water goes 2/3 into the ICF; hypotonic fluid moves water into cells.
  • C: water into brain cells worsens cerebral edema and raises ICP; these patients need isotonic or hypertonic fluid.
  • D: normal plasma osmolality is about 285-295 mOsm/kg, not 380-390.
  • E: 3% saline is for symptomatic hyponatremia; free water deficits (hypernatremia) get D5W.

Her skin is cold and clammy and there is pitting edema to the knees bilaterally. She is using accessory muscles to breathe and can only speak 1-2 words at a time. The correct answer is B.

stem: A 16-year-old female presents to the ED after overdosing on her father’s diltiazem. Her vitals are as follows: HR – 26, SBP – 63, RR – 24, T – 37.0°C, O2 sat – unable to detect. Which type of circulatory shock does she primarily have?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 1). Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine CCB. The lecture says it blocks myocardial as well as smooth-muscle Ca2+ channels, slowing the SA/AV nodes and reducing contractility. In overdose that means severe bradycardia (HR 26) and pump failure: a primarily cardiogenic shock.

  • A: there is no volume loss (hypovolemic shock is the hemorrhagic or dehydration kind, 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock).
  • B: toxic shock syndrome is a toxin-mediated infection, not drug toxicity.
  • C: vasodilation contributes, and dominates in dihydropyridine overdose (amlodipine, with reflex tachycardia), but a heart rate of 26 points to the pump.
  • E: nothing is obstructing flow (no tamponade, PE or tension pneumothorax).

stem: A 58-year-old presents to the ED with 2 days of generalized abdominal pain and copious vomiting. His last bowel movement was 3 days ago and was normal. stem: A 32-year-old is involved in a high-speed rollover motor vehicle collision. Vitals are as follows: HR – 119, BP – 108/84, RR – 24, T – 36.9°C, O2 sat – 96% on room air. His extremities are cool and cap refill is 3 seconds. Which of the following is TRUE?

This patient likely has neurogenic shock
Urine output is useful indicator of shock in the initial assessment
This patient has likely lost up to 15% of blood volume
This patient is in class II hemorrhagic shock

The correct answer is E.

From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). Match his vitals to the class table: HR 119 (100-120), BP normal but pulse pressure narrowed (24), RR 24 (20-30), cool with delayed refill.   • D: up to 15% is class I, with a pulse under 100.

stem: A 52-year-old presented to the ED with a massive upper GI bleed due to esophageal varices. Treatment was with 15 units of packed red blood cells. Which additional treatments/measures would NOT have been indicated specifically to avoid “the lethal triad”?

options.html: Warmed blood products given via a rapid transfuser
Blood gases after every 6-8 units of red blood cells

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). The lethal triad is acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy, and each distractor is a named countermeasure to one arm of it:

  • A warmed products via a rapid transfuser (Level I warmer) - prevents hypothermia.
  • B, D platelets and plasma - offset the dilutional coagulopathy that worsens progressively at 10, 20, 30 units of pRBC.
  • E serial blood gases - track the acidosis that cripples Ca-dependent clotting complexes (rFVIIa activity falls 90% at pH 7.0).
  • C intubation may well be needed in a massive variceal bleed for airway protection, but that is an airway indication, not a measure against the triad - hence the answer.

stem: A 71-year-old presents to the ED with confusion and abdominal pain. Vitals are as follows: HR – 119, BP – 84/63, RR – 24, T – 38.1°C, O2 sat – 95% on room air. Initial bloodwork: CBC – within normal limits, remaining bloodwork is pending. Does this patient likely have sepsis?

Cannot be determined until the rest of the bloodwork is back
No, because MAP is greater than 65
Cannot be determined until response to IV crystalloid is known

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection, and the lecture lists the bedside signs: confusion (brain), tachypnea (lung), hypotension and tachycardia. A febrile patient with abdominal pain has a presumed infection, and she already shows altered mentation, RR 24 and SBP 84 - all three qSOFA items - so A is right.

  • D: MAP is about 70 here, but a MAP above 65 does not exclude sepsis; MAP 65 is the septic-shock vasopressor target, not a sepsis criterion.

stem: A 20-year-old presents to the ED with 2 days of sore throat and fever. Clinical examination suggests possible streptococcal pharyngitis. GCS is normal and capillary refill is 2 seconds. Vitals are as follows: HR – 122, BP – 125/82, RR – 23, T – 39.1°C, O2 sat – 98% on room air. WBC – 18 (N 4-10), venous blood gases: pH – 7.35 (7.32-7.42), lactate 1.1 (N 0.9 – 2.4). Does this patient likely have sepsis?

options.html: Yes, because she has at least 2 SIRS criteria
No, because SBP is greater than 100
No, because her compensatory responses appear adaptive
Uncertain, because cannot determine sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score
Yes, because a bacterial etiology is suspected

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). The lecture defines sepsis (Sepsis-3) as life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. This patient has a likely strep pharyngitis and every SIRS item (HR 122, RR 23, T 39.1, WBC 18), but no organ dysfunction: GCS normal, cap refill 2 s, BP 125/82, pH and lactate normal. Her tachycardia and fever are an appropriate, adaptive response to a local infection, so C is right.

  • A: SIRS criteria were dropped from the sepsis definition because they flag exactly this kind of healthy inflammatory response.
  • B: SBP is not the discriminator; organ dysfunction is.
  • D: a formal SOFA score is not needed at the bedside - the lecture notes it is mostly a trial tool - and the clinical picture already shows no failing organ.
  • E: a bacterial infection alone is not sepsis.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to the ED with large, painful patch of redness on his upper extremity. He is confused and appears unwell. Initial vitals: HR – 116, BP – 72/38, RR – 20, T – 35.5°C, O2 sat – 95% on room air. For his initial treatment, he was placed on a cardiorespiratory monitor, and two large bore IVs were established. Bloodwork (including blood cultures) was sent, and he was given 30 ml/kg of Ringer’s lactate, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. The WBC count was 2.0 (N 4-10). Initial serum lactate was 3.8 (N 0.9-2.2) and post IV fluid boluses, it’s now 3.5. Repeat vitals: HR – 115, BP – 82/40, RR – 20, T – 35.6°C, O2 sat – 95% on room air. Does this patient likely have septic shock?

options.html: Yes, because the serum lactate is elevated
Yes, because he has persistent hypotension and elevated lactate despite adequate IV fluids
No, because he is not febrile, and WBC count is low
Uncertain because blood culture results are pending
Uncertain because inadequate IV fluids have been provided

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). The lecture defines septic shock as hypotension that does not respond to fluids (arteriolar vasodilation plus capillary leak), which is why vasopressors are added. After a full 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus he is still 82/40 with lactate 3.5, so B is right; the Sepsis-3 definition adds the persistent lactate above 2.

  • A: an elevated lactate alone is hypoperfusion, not septic shock; it is the pairing with fluid-refractory hypotension that defines it.
  • C: hypothermia and leukopenia are markers of severe sepsis - the lecture lists hypothermia or fever - and they worsen the prognosis.
  • D: cultures are not required to diagnose or treat; antibiotics must not wait on them.
  • E: 30 mL/kg is the standard adequate initial bolus.

stem: What is the goal of CPR?

options.html: To increase venous return to the heart
To maintain cerebral perfusion for optimal neurological outcome
To determine cause of cardiac arrest
To kill time until EMS arrives

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Compressions do not restart the heart; they generate enough forward flow to keep the brain and heart perfused until a definitive therapy (defibrillation, reversal of the cause) can work. Survival that matters is survival with intact neurological function, so C.

  • A: ROSC is the goal of the whole resuscitation - shocks, drugs, treating Hs and Ts - not of CPR alone.
  • B: venous return during recoil is a mechanism of CPR, not its purpose.
  • D: finding the cause is a parallel task for the team.
  • E: it is active treatment, not a holding pattern.

Defibrillation is the delivery of a random shock

stem: Indicate which statements are false regarding the mechanism of epinephrine?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 1). Epinephrine is a mixed alpha and beta agonist, and the lecture's receptor table says beta-1 raises HR, contractility and conduction velocity. So B is the false statement: epinephrine increases contractility, it does not decrease it.

  • A: true - alpha-1 gives vasoconstriction, the effect that matters in arrest (coronary perfusion pressure).
  • C: true - beta-1 and beta-2 agonism.
  • D: true - beta-2 relaxes smooth muscle, giving bronchodilation (why it treats anaphylaxis).
  • E: true - alpha vasoconstriction plus beta-1 inotropy/chronotropy raise BP.

stem: Which of the following statements are true regarding amiodarone?

options.html: Amiodarone prolongs that action potential and refractory period in myocardial tissue
Amiodarone is an alpha receptor agonist
Amiodarone increases ROSC and survival to hospital in OHCA
Amiodarone has been shown to improve neurological outcomes in OHCA
The first dose of amiodarone in the ACLS algorithm is 150 mg IV bolus

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5). Amiodarone is class III: it blocks K+ channels in phase 3, prolonging the plateau, action potential and refractory period (hence the long QT), so A is true.

  • B: false - it is not an agonist; the lecture notes it has class I, II, III and IV effects, i.e. beta- and Ca2+-blocking actions.
  • C: in OHCA trials it improved survival to admission, not survival to discharge (see flag).
  • D: false - no neurological outcome benefit has been shown.
  • E: false - the first arrest dose is 300 mg IV/IO; 150 mg is the second dose (and the stable-VT bolus).

stem: T or F: lidocaine is effective in terminating VF/pVT
answer:
T

From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5). True, in the sense the arrest algorithm uses it. Lidocaine (class IB, rapid-onset Na+ channel block) is highly specific for ventricular myocytes, so it only works on ventricular arrhythmias. The lecture puts it alongside amiodarone for shock-refractory VF/pVT, and notes that lidocaine given with defibrillation improves the chance the heart restarts after a failed shock.

  • The shock does the terminating; lidocaine makes the next shock more likely to succeed and helps prevent recurrence.
  • Contrast: lidocaine does not slow AF or treat SVT, because it has no nodal action.

stem: Which of the following are priorities in the initial phase of post-arrest care?

options.html: Advanced airway + point of care glucose check
Maintaining SBP > 90 mm Hg + obtaining a 12 lead ECG
Inducing hypothermia to 30 C for TTM
Continuous monitoring of core temperature + SpO2 >/= 94%

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Once ROSC is achieved, the first job is keeping the patient alive and finding the cause: treat hypotension (SBP at least 90 mmHg, MAP at least 65) and get a 12-lead ECG straight away, because STEMI sends the patient for emergent coronary angiography. The option text lost its inequality signs in extraction; read B as 'SBP of at least 90'.

  • A: securing the airway belongs early, but glucose is managed in the later critical-care phase.
  • C: 30°C is below any TTM target (32-36°C).
  • D: EEG monitoring is for the comatose patient in the ICU phase.
  • E: core temperature monitoring belongs to the TTM/ICU phase; the oxygen target is part of the first steps, but the pairing does not.

stem: In post-arrest induced hypothermia, what is the goal temperature?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Targeted temperature management after ROSC in a comatose patient aims for a constant temperature somewhere in 32-36°C for at least 24 hours, then prevention of fever. The protective effect comes from lowering cerebral metabolic demand and reperfusion injury; below about 32°C, arrhythmias, coagulopathy and infection outweigh the benefit.

  • A, C: 30-32°C and 31°C fall below the recommended floor.
  • D: 34°C is in range, which is presumably what the source taught.
  • B: 33°C is also in range (and was one arm of the TTM trial), see flag.

stem: Which physician groups provide care for trauma patients?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Trauma care is a continuum that runs well past the trauma bay, so every group listed has a role:

  • A: physiatrists (PM&R) lead rehabilitation after TBI, spinal cord injury, amputation and polytrauma.
  • B: primary care physicians do injury prevention (counselling, screening for intimate partner violence and falls risk), provide rural first-contact stabilization, and handle long-term follow-up.
  • C: psychiatrists manage acute stress disorder, PTSD, substance use and self-harm, which both cause and follow injury.

So D.

stem: Injury is the leading cause of death for:

options.html: All males below the age of 65

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Injury (unintentional plus intentional: motor vehicle collisions, poisonings/overdose, falls, suicide, homicide) is the leading cause of death from age 1 to 44. Older adults die mostly of cancer and cardiovascular disease, and infants mostly of perinatal and congenital causes, which is why the band starts at 1 and ends at 44.

  • A: overgeneralized - marginalized groups carry a disproportionate injury burden, but injury is not the leading cause of death for all of them at all ages.
  • B: in males aged 45-64, cancer and heart disease overtake injury.
  • D: a distractor with no population statistic behind it.

stem: What is the most important component of the primary survey? In other words, which one would you put first if you were redoing the order today?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The trend in trauma is to move catastrophic hemorrhage control ahead of the airway (xABCDE / 'C-ABC', MARCH). The reason: exsanguination kills in minutes, and most preventable trauma deaths are from bleeding. A tourniquet or direct pressure takes seconds and must not wait on intubation, and an induction for intubation in an under-resuscitated patient can cause arrest.

  • A: still first in classic ATLS teaching and in non-hemorrhagic patients, but an airway is useless without circulating blood.
  • B: tension pneumothorax is decompressed quickly, but it is a less common killer than hemorrhage.
  • D: neurological status is assessed only after perfusion is restored.

stem: How much blood do you need to lose to definitively become hypotensive?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). The lecture's class table keeps BP normal through class II (up to 1500 mL, 30%) and only shows a falling BP in class III (1500-2000 mL, 30-40%). 1600 mL is the only option past that threshold.

  • A: 500 mL is class I (up to 750 mL), where vitals are essentially normal.
  • B, C: 800 and 1200 mL are class II. HR rises to 100-120 and pulse pressure narrows, but BP is preserved.

Hypotension is a late sign, and the young patient compensates longest.

stem: All of the following are appropriate steps to control bleeding from a pelvic fracture except:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Pelvic hemorrhage comes mainly from the venous plexus and cancellous bone, plus some arterial branches of the internal iliac, deep in the pelvis. A tourniquet cannot compress it: tourniquets work only on extremity wounds proximal to the bleed, so A is the exception.

  • B: preperitoneal packing tamponades venous and bony bleeding directly.
  • C: external fixation (like a pelvic binder at the bedside) closes the pelvic volume and stabilizes the bone ends, which reduces bleeding.
  • D: angioembolization treats the arterial source (contrast blush on CT).

The 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock principle applies throughout: resuscitation buys time, but stopping the bleeding is the treatment.

stem: A total of ____ of blood out of a chest tube constitutes a massive hemothorax and mandates surgical exploration
answer:
The correct answer is D.

A massive hemothorax is defined by at least 1500 mL of blood on initial chest tube insertion, or ongoing output of about 200 mL/h for 2-4 hours. Either means a major vessel or lung-parenchyma bleed that the tube will not control, so the patient needs thoracotomy.

  • A, B, C: 500-1200 mL can come from chest-wall or minor lung bleeding that stops once the lung re-expands and apposes the pleura. Watch the drain rate and the patient's hemodynamics, but these volumes alone do not mandate surgery.

Physiologically, 1500 mL is 30% of blood volume, the class III threshold where BP falls (06 - Hemorrhagic Shock).

stem: At and below what score on the Glasgow Coma Scale is intubation recommended for airway protection?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From Schulich Reviews - Neuro (PoM 2). The rule is 'GCS 8, intubate'. At a GCS of 8 or less the patient cannot reliably protect the airway (loss of gag and cough, risk of aspiration). They are also at risk of hypoxia and hypercapnia, which raise ICP in the injured brain. GCS 3-8 is also the review's definition of severe TBI, so the intubation threshold and the severe band coincide.

  • Higher cut-offs (9-13) are moderate TBI, managed with close observation rather than routine intubation.
  • Lower cut-offs would wait until the airway is already lost.

stem: This osmotic agent both expands extracellular volume and reduces intracranial pressure:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Both osmotic agents lower ICP by drawing water out of brain tissue across an intact blood-brain barrier (10 - Neurosurgical Emergencies, PoM 2 Neuro; the Schulich Reviews - Neuro list 23.4% and 3% saline). What separates them is what happens to the circulation:

  • C: hypertonic saline (3%, about 500 mmol/L NaCl per 13 - IV Fluids) stays in the ECF and pulls water into it, so it expands intravascular volume while it lowers ICP. That makes it the choice in the hypotensive trauma patient.
  • A: mannitol acts by osmotic diuresis. It lowers ICP but then contracts the ECF and can drop BP.
  • B: sorbitol is not used for ICP.
  • D: normal saline expands the ECF but has no osmotic gradient, so it does not reduce ICP.

stem: “Bullet Math” refers to the detailed assessment of both ballistic wounds and retained projectiles seen on imaging in order to:

options.html: Establish an odd number of wounds and projectiles and estimate likely trajectories
Establish an even number of wounds and projectiles and estimate likely trajectories
Establish an odd number of wounds and projectiles and estimate caliber of bullet
Establish an even number of wounds and projectiles and estimate caliber of bullet

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Each bullet either passes through the body, leaving an entry and an exit wound, or stays inside, leaving one wound and one retained projectile. Either way it contributes two items to the count, so wounds + retained projectiles should add up to an even number. Pairing them lets you reconstruct each trajectory and predict which structures lie in its path.

  • A, C: an odd total is the warning sign: a missed wound (axilla, perineum, scalp, back) or a missed projectile, which should prompt a repeat survey or more imaging.
  • C, D: calibre cannot be reliably estimated from wound size or imaging appearance, and it does not change management; trajectory does.

stem: Exsanguinating extremity wounds in patients with profound shock are best initially managed with:

options.html: Blind clamping of vessels deep within wound

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A proximal tourniquet stops arterial extremity hemorrhage in seconds, with no special skill and no need to see into the wound. In profound shock, every minute of bleeding feeds the lethal triad (06 - Hemorrhagic Shock, PoM 2 Repro), and 'stop the bleeding' is the treatment.

  • A: closing the skin hides the bleed; blood keeps collecting beneath it (and compartment syndrome can follow).
  • B: blind clamping in a bloody field seldom catches the vessel and injures adjacent nerves and veins. Clamping is done under direct vision in the OR.
  • D: amputation is a late decision for an unsalvageable limb, not initial hemorrhage control.

stem: The term FAST refers to:

options.html: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma
Thoracoabdominal sonographic testing to detect blood in the chest, pericardium, peritoneal cavity, and retroperitoneal space
An assessment by ultrasound for trauma that should be completed within 5 minutes of arrival for all trauma patients

answer:
The correct answer is A.

FAST stands for Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a bedside look for free fluid (presumed blood) in the pericardium, RUQ (Morison's pouch), LUQ and pelvis; eFAST adds the chest for pneumothorax and hemothorax.

  • B: 'abdominal' is wrong - the pericardial view is a core part of it.
  • C: FAST is poor at detecting retroperitoneal blood (e.g. pelvic fracture, renal or aortic bleeding), so it cannot claim to test that space.
  • D: it is an adjunct to the primary survey when indicated (typically the unstable patient). There is no rule that every trauma patient gets one within 5 minutes.

stem: In patients with minor head injury, all of the following findings would predict the need for CT imaging except:

options.html: Vomiting at least once in the ED
GCS score < 15 more than 2 hours after injury
Any sign of basal skull fracture

answer:
The correct answer is A.

This is the Canadian CT Head Rule for minor head injury (GCS 13-15 with witnessed LOC, amnesia or disorientation). Its high-risk criteria are: GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, any sign of basal skull fracture, vomiting at least twice, and age 65 or older.

  • A: a single episode of vomiting does not meet the threshold of two, so A is the exception.
  • B: read as 'age of at least 65' (the inequality sign was lost in extraction).
  • C: read as 'GCS below 15 at 2 hours'. As printed ('GCS score 15') it would not predict anything, so this too is a lost sign.
  • D: the signs are hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, Battle's sign and CSF oto- or rhinorrhea.

stem: With respect to vascular access in patients with hemorrhagic shock, which of the following is true:

options.html: If extra access is required a second or even third intraosseous (IO) line should be placed
Administering blood through multiple peripheral IVs simultaneously is appropriate
A 14 gauge peripheral IV cannula should almost always be able to be placed by an experienced provider even in patients with severe shock

A single large bore, central venous introducer sheath connected to a rapid infusion device and served by a crew of providers dedicated exclusively to administering blood products is the optimal approach

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Flow through a cannula rises with the fourth power of its radius and falls with its length. A short, very wide central introducer sheath on a rapid infuser therefore outflows several peripheral lines. A dedicated blood-product team keeps track of products, ratios, warming and calcium instead of leaving them to the resuscitation leader.

  • A: IO access is a bridge; its flow is limited, and multiple IOs do not match a large-bore central line.
  • B: several uncoordinated peripheral lines make it hard to track what was given and to warm it, and each small line flows slowly.
  • C: in severe shock, peripheral veins collapse and a 14 G often cannot be placed, even by experts.

The 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock lecture starts with large-bore IV x2 and escalates to central lines.

Administration of cryoprecipitate or recombinant fibrinogen concentrate should generally be given to any massively bleeding patient with a fibrinogen less than

  1. 0 b.
  2. 5 c.
  3. 0 d. 2.5
answer:
From 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient (FoM Block 3, Week 10). In massive bleeding, the lecture's MTP flow adds early fibrinogen replacement (fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate; 10 units of cryo gives about 4 g) and TXA, guided later by fibrinogen levels. Fibrinogen is the first factor to fall to critical levels in hemorrhage and dilution. The usual trigger is a fibrinogen below 1.5 g/L (some protocols use 1.5-2.0, and 2.0 in obstetric hemorrhage).

  • A cut-off of 1.0 g/L is the older, now-too-late threshold.
  • A cut-off of 2.5 g/L sits within the normal range (about 2-4 g/L) and would over-treat.

stem: Injury prevention is a practice that is primarily in the domain of:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Injury is predictable and preventable, and the opportunities to prevent it arise in every specialty, so prevention belongs to all physicians. Examples: car seats and safe sleep in paediatrics, falls risk and deprescribing in geriatrics, intimate partner violence screening in obstetrics, and driving fitness with seizures or dementia in neurology and family medicine.

  • A: family physicians do much of the counselling, but they do not own the field.
  • B: trauma surgeons see the result and often advocate, but they meet patients after the injury has happened.
  • C: obstetricians have a real but narrow role (IPV in pregnancy, seatbelt use).

stem: What is the one drug level that should be drawn on all intentional overdose patients?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Acetaminophen is the one level drawn on every intentional overdose, whatever the patient says they took. Four reasons: it is commonly co-ingested and under-reported; it is asymptomatic early; the hepatotoxicity is delayed (it is the commonest cause of acute liver failure, per 05 - Acute Hepatitis, PoM 1 GI); and an effective antidote, N-acetylcysteine, works best if given early. A 4-hour level plotted on the nomogram decides treatment.

  • A, C, D: carbamazepine, quetiapine and digoxin levels are drawn only when that ingestion is suspected, and quetiapine levels are not clinically useful.
  • B: methanol is screened indirectly (osmolal gap, AGMA) and only on suspicion.

stem: What is the formula for calculating the Anion Gap?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 11 - Acid Base Disturbances (PoM 1 GU, Week 14). The anion gap is the main cation minus the two main measured anions: Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-), normally about 12, made up mostly of albumin. Lower the expected gap by about 3 for every 10 g/L that albumin falls below 40.

  • A: doubling Na+ belongs to the osmolality formula, not the gap.
  • B: 2Na + urea (BUN) + glucose is the calculated serum osmolality, used for the osmolal gap in toxic alcohol ingestion.
  • D: adding the anions gives a sum, not a gap.
  • E: subtracting Cl- from HCO3- inverts the sign and is meaningless.

stem: Where does the term toxidrome come from?

options.html: A specific ECG finding in digoxin overdose

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 09 - Cholinergic Pharmacology (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 1).   • D: a toxidrome is a clinical pattern across drug classes, not an ECG sign of one drug.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a symptom of anticholinergic toxicity?
answer:

stem: What is most likely to rapid lead to death in patients with sympathomimetic toxicity?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

In sympathomimetic toxicity (cocaine, amphetamines), agitation, muscle activity, seizures and vasoconstriction generate heat and stop it escaping. Hyperthermia is the sign that kills quickly: core temperatures above about 41°C cause rhabdomyolysis, DIC, multi-organ failure and death within hours, which is why rapid cooling and sedation are the priority.

  • A Tachycardia and D hypertension: dangerous (ischemia, dissection, bleed) but usually respond to sedation; temperature is the best predictor of death.
  • B Diaphoresis: helps dissipate heat, it is not itself lethal.
  • C Altered mental status: drives the heat production but is not the direct killer.

stem: What is the first line drug used to treat sympathomimetic toxicity?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Benzodiazepines treat the cause: they calm the CNS stimulation that drives the agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, heat production and seizures, and they are the anticonvulsant for sympathomimetic seizures.

  • E Propofol: an option for refractory agitation after intubation, not first line.

stem: An 88-year-old man is brought in by EMS with decreased level of consciousness and tachypnea. His wife says he has been unwell for the last two days. His medications include atorvastatin and ASA. His HR 116, BP 90/75, RR 26, 94% RA. He is rousable to voice. His labs return: CBC normal, pH 7.15, pCO2 20, Bicarb 10, Na 133, Cl 98, Cr 377, INR 1.1, ALT 89, ASA 2.8 mmol/L, Ethanol 35 mmol/L, APAP negative. What is the best option for treatment?

options.html: Start bicarbonate therapy, admit to hospital
Start broad spectrum antibiotics, admit to hospital
Start bicarbonate therapy, consult nephrology for hemodialysis

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From the salicylate (asprin overdose) reference note and 11 - Acid Base Disturbances (PoM 1 GU, Week 14). The lecture's salicylate patient is alkalemic from the added respiratory alkalosis; this man is acidemic (pH 7.15), confused, and in renal failure (Cr 377), so he cannot excrete the drug. That is severe poisoning, the note's indication for hemodialysis, with bicarbonate started while it is arranged. An elderly chronic ASA user with confusion and tachypnea is the classic missed chronic salicylism.

  • A: NAC treats acetaminophen, which is negative.
  • B: bicarbonate alone relies on urinary excretion that his kidneys cannot provide.
  • C: chronic salicylism mimics sepsis, but the level explains the picture; antibiotics miss the cause.

stem: Which of the following clinical signs are NOT consistent with salicylate toxicity?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From the salicylate (asprin overdose) reference note and 11 - Acid Base Disturbances (PoM 1 GU, Week 14). Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory centre, causing hyperventilation and a primary respiratory alkalosis on top of the AGMA. Tachypnea/hyperpnea is expected, so bradypnea does not fit (it would suggest a co-ingested depressant or a pre-arrest patient).

  • B Tinnitus: the classic early sign, listed in the moderate tier.
  • C Vomiting: nausea and vomiting appear even in mild toxicity.
  • D Confusion: moderate to severe toxicity (then delirium, seizures, coma).

stem: Salicylates are known to interfere with the production of ATP. This is because salicylates:

options.html: Block complex 1 of the electron transport chain
Cause cellular hypoxia leading to failure of the electron transport chain

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Salicylate is a weak acid that carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, dissipating the proton gradient that ATP synthase uses: it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation. The electron transport chain keeps running, so O2 is consumed and energy is released as heat instead of ATP, which explains the fever, increased CO2 production, anaerobic shift and lactic acidosis.

  • A: salicylate does not consume phosphate.
  • C: complex I blockade is the rotenone/metformin-type mechanism, which stops electron flow rather than uncoupling it.
  • D: oxygen supply is intact; the defect is in using the gradient, not in hypoxia.

stem: A medical toxicologist is:

options.html: A physician who has a special interest in toxicology and has taken an online course
A trained nurse or pharmacist who provides information on poisoning
A person who works in a lab studying the effect of toxins on the human body
A physician who has graduated from an accredited post-graduate medical education fellowship pertaining to the field of toxicology and pharmacology

answer:
The correct answer is D.

A medical toxicologist is a physician who has completed formal, accredited postgraduate training in toxicology (in Canada, usually a fellowship after emergency medicine, internal medicine, pediatrics or similar). They provide bedside and poison-centre consultation for poisoned patients.

  • A: interest plus an online course is not a credential; the title implies accredited training.
  • B: nurses and pharmacists staffing poison centres are specialists in poison information, not medical toxicologists.
  • C: a laboratory scientist studying toxins is a toxicologist in the research sense, not a medical one.

stem: Poison Centres are involved in all of the following EXCEPT:

options.html: Gathering epidemiologic data on trends in toxic exposures and poisonings
Providing medical advise to bedside physicians caring for poisoned patients
Providing telephone advise to the general public on poisonings and toxic exposures
Researching and educating the general public in poisoning prevention

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Poison centres are public-health services: they advise, track and educate about poisonings. They have no role in making drugs, so pharmaceutical development and production is the exception.

  • B: calls are logged, which makes poison centres a main source of epidemiologic data on exposure trends.
  • C: they give specialist advice (with a medical toxicologist on call) to clinicians treating poisoned patients.
  • D: public telephone advice is their core service, and it keeps many exposures out of the ED.
  • E: prevention research and public education are part of the mandate.

stem: A 21-year-old man is dropped off at the ED by friends after being stabbed in the thigh. The patient's jeans are soaked with blood. On examination his vitals are as follows: HR - 137, BP - 76/38, RR - 24, O2 sat - 98% on room air, T - 37.3°C PO The nurse has placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor, established 2 large bore IVs, and has given a 1 L bolus of Ringer's lactate. Despite application of a tourniquet and direct pressure, the wound keeps bleeding briskly. What is your next best step?

options.html: Give crossmatched packed cells when available
Give another 1L bolus of Ringer's lactate

answer: The correct answer is D. D; Airway and Breathing are satisfactory. There is no need to intubate. Circulation is not - this patient is in hemorrhagic shock. Aside from trying to prevent ongoing blood loss, you need to replace blood loss. Initially it is acceptable to use crystalloid to expand the intravascular space, but more than 1L is not recommended as crystalloid does not have oxygen carrying capacity. This patient has not responded adequately to the 1L bolus of Ringer's lactate and he is still bleeding. You should not wait for crossmatched packed cells, this takes too much time. This patient is very sick. You also should not await CBC results, as the Hb will not be reflective of acute blood loss, so should not guide management, and will only result in dangerous delays.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents to the ED with abdominal pain and heavy vaginal bleeding. The gestational age is approximately 7 weeks according to her last menstrual period. Her vital signs are: HR - 129, BP - 75/34, RR - 22, T - 37.1°C, O2 sat - 99% on room air She is awake and speaking to you, and there are no signs of airway obstruction. Auscultation of the chest is clear, and heart sounds are normal. She looks unwell, her skin is pale and capillary refill is delayed. Palpation of the abdomen reveals significant left lower quadrant tenderness. The patient has been placed on a cardiorespiratory monitor by nursing staff. What is your best NEXT step in managing this patient?

options.html: Obtain 2 large bore peripheral IV lines
Perform a bedside ultrasound looking for intra-abdominal free fluid
Obtain a formal ultrasound looking for ectopic pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is A. A; This patient is in shock. There are no immediate concerns re: airway and breathing so no current role for intubation or provision of supplementary oxygen. There is a concern re: circulation. Establish 2 large bore peripheral IV lines and start fluid resuscitation ASAP. It is a reasonable step after that to perform a bedside ultrasound. You would only consider getting a formal ultrasound to look for ectopic pregnancy if the patient stabilized, and it was still needed after PoCUS. A formal ultrasound involves transferring the patient outside of the ED where it is difficult and dangerous to manage an unstable patient.

stem: A 35-year-old female is involved in a high-speed motor vehicle crash. She is brought to the ED via ambulance. She complains of shortness of breath and left lower extremity pain. Her vitals are as follows: HR - 129, BP - 81/43, RR - 30, T - 36.5°C, O2 sat - 94% on non-rebreather. Identify an injury you might expect to find during the secondary survey.
answer: The correct answer is A. A; Injuries you might find on the primary survey include flail chest, mid-shaft femur fracture, unstable pelvic fracture, hemoperitoneum on FAST. She has clinical signs consistent with any of these injuries. A foot fracture is not generally found during the primary survey, as it is not a life or limb threatening injury.

stem: A 50-year-old male is brought to the ED several hours after a suspected intentional ingestion. He complains of nausea, vomiting and tinnitus. Shortly after arriving in the ED, he has a seizure. His vitals are as follows: HR - 118, BP - 148/92, RR - 30, T - 38.5°C, O2 sat - 93% on room air. Toxicity from which over the counter medication could BEST account for his clinical presentation?
answer: The correct answer is B. B; The only over the counter medication listed here the would cause fever, tachypnea, altered mental status/seizure and tinnitus would be ASA. Gravol and Benadryl could cause some similar symptoms, but tinnitus is unique to ASA.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with retrosternal chest pain after shovelling snow. He has a sudden loss of consciousness while you are taking the history. You cannot detect a pulse. The monitor shows the attached. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
answer: The correct answer is B. B; The monitor shows VT. There is no pulse. If the crash cart is ready to go, defibrillate immediately. Cardioversion is only for rhythms with a pulse. IV amiodarone would only be later in the arrest sequence if defibrillation was unsuccessful. There is no role for IV NTG in pulseless patients. While MI may the underlying cause for the cardiac arrest, thrombolysis is not part of the initial cardiac arrest sequence.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents to the ED with a complaint of dysuria, frequency and urgency. He also feels generally unwell with lethargy and nausea. His vitals are as follows: HR - 128, BP - 82/50, RR - 22, O2 sat 95% on room air, T 38.6°C PO A nurse has placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor and established a large bore IV. Which of the following outlines the most appropriate next steps in management of this patient:

options.html: Blood cultures, 2nd large bore IV, NS bolus 1 L IV, urine culture, piperacillin-tazobactam IV
Blood cultures, NS bolus 1L IV, urine culture, ampicillin IV
Blood cultures, Ringer's lactate 1 L IV, urine culture, metronidazole IV
Blood cultures, 2nd large bore IV, Ringer's lactate 500 cc IV, urine culture, lumbar puncture, azithromycin IV
Blood cultures, oral fluid challenge, urine culture, ciprofloxacin PO

answer: The correct answer is A. A; The patient has signs suggestive of sepsis (hypotension and tachypnea) in the setting of infection. The symptoms suggest a potential urinary tract source. Treatment of poor perfusion should be with 2 large bore IVs and at least 1L crystalloid bolus (NS or Ringer's). It is prudent to start broad spectrum parenteral antibiotics such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ideally after obtaining blood cultures and a urine culture. Ampicillin, metronidazole and azithromycin are parenteral antibiotics, but not broad enough coverage, and have incomplete coverage of urinary pathogens as well. Oral fluids and antibiotics are not the first line treatment recommendations for sepsis.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 hours of chest pain and shortness of breath. His vital signs are as follows: HR - 80, BP - 95/42, RR - 24, T - 37.1°C, O2 sat - 96%. A stat EKG is ordered and is attached. Which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.html: The EKG is diagnostic for an inferior STEMI
The EKG has evidence of reciprocal changes
The lesion is likely in the right coronary artery
Up to 3 sprays of sublingual nitroglycerine should be initiated
A 15 lead EKG should be ordered and can include the following leads: V4R, V8, V9

answer: The correct answer is D. D; The EKG is diagnostic for an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF). There are reciprocal changes (ST depression in the lateral leads (I, aVL). The lesion is likely in the right coronary artery, as that is most common cause of inferior STEMI. A 15 lead should be ordered to assess for RV and posterior myocardial involvement. NTG spray should not be initiated as blood pressure is already on the low side, and if this patient has RV infarction, they will get profoundly hypotensive with preload reduction.

stem: You are called to assess a 75-year-old woman on the ward with a complaint of shortness of breath. She is post-operative day 7 from a debulking surgery for ovarian cancer. She has had no chest pain, nor cough or fever. On examination her vitals are: HR - 119, BP - 128/85, RR - 28, T - 36.8°C, O2 sat - 95%. Her chest is clear bilaterally and heart sounds are normal. There is no swelling, redness or tenderness in her legs. Which test is NOT indicated in this patient to help clarify the diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. E; The clinical findings of tachycardia, dyspnea, and normal breath sounds in a patient who is both post-operative from surgery and has cancer, all strongly point towards a diagnosis of PE. If you were to calculate her Well's Score, it would be greater than 4, so using a d-dimer would be inappropriate. A D-dimer can only be used to exclude PE in patients who are low risk for PE. A CXR, Point of Care Ultrasound (heart, lungs), EKG and CT pulmonary angiogram would all be appropriate tests to rule in/out the suspected diagnosis.

stem: A 63-year-old female presents to the ED with an 8-hour history of chest heaviness and shortness of breath. On examination his vitals are: HR - 75, BP - 100/55, RR - 30, T - 36.5 ºC, O2 sat 72% on room air. She is diaphoretic, grey and appears anxious. She is sitting in the tripod position and using accessory muscles to breath. Auscultation of the chest reveals diffuse crackles bilaterally. Heart sounds are normal. JVP is elevated. Extremities are poorly perfused, and ankles are edematous. This patient is in shock. Classify it:
answer: The correct answer is B. B; While hypotension and poor peripheral perfusion are typical of obstructive, cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock, an elevated JVP is typical for obstructive and cardiogenic shock. Pulmonary edema is more typical for cardiogenic shock. The patient also has chest heaviness, which suggests a potential cardiac etiology. Septic shock is a form of distributive shock. Distributed shock has warm, well perfused periphery due to inappropriate vasodilation.

stem: A 19-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by paramedics from home with decreased level of consciousness. He was at work earlier in the day (auto repair shop) and came home early complaining of feeling unwell. He was vomiting and complaining of flank pain. One hour later he was found unresponsive by his mother. On exam he is moaning to pain, but otherwise unresponsive. With stimulation he withdraws his arms and legs. Vitals: Heart rate 124, regular Respiratory rate 36 Oxygen saturation 100% on oxygen by mask Blood pressure 88/54 Temperature 37.4°C Laboratory: Hemoglobin 154 g/L (normal range 120 -150 g/L) White blood count: 16.2 x 109/L (normal 4 -10 x 109/L) Platelets 368 x 109/L (normal 150 -400 x 109/L) INR: 1.1 (normal 0.9 -1.1) PTT: 28 s (normal 25 -27 s) Sodium 146 (normal 135 -145 mmol/L) Potassium 4 (normal 3.5 -5.5 mmol/L) Chloride 108 (normal 98 -108 mmol/L) Bicarbonate 8 (normal 22 -29 mmol/L) Lactate 3.4 (normal 0.9 -2.4 mmol/L) Urea 13.1 (normal high 8.3 mmol/L) Creatinine 168 (normal 40 -150 mmol/L) Glucose 8.9 (normal 3.4 -8 mmol/L) Blood gases: pO2: 248 on oxygen by mask pCO2: 16 HCO3: 7 pH: 7.08 Osmolality: 340 Urinalysis: crystals seen Based on the information provided what is the most likely cause of this patient's illness?
answer: The correct answer is D. D; All of the substances listed can cause altered mental status. You should have calculated the Anion Gap and Osmolar gap and found that both are elevated. The blood gases also confirm a metabolic acidosis. All of this should lead you to consider toxic alcohols. The crystals in the urine point towards ethylene glycol specifically.

stem: A 48-year-old female presents after overdosing on her antidepressant medication. She is lethargic on arrival. Her vitals are: HR 110, BP 108/70, RR 24, O2 saturation 97% on room air, T 37°C oral Shortly after arrival she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Post-seizure her GCS is 6, and this does not improve over the ensuing 30 minutes. An ECG is ordered that shows a wide QRS. Which is NOT indicated in this patient?
answer: The correct answer is C. C; The clinical signs in this case all point towards TCA overdose. Antidepressant medication, altered mental status, seizure, wide QRS. Treatment of TCAs is with sodium bicarb for wide QRS / wide complex tachycardia, and benzodiazepines for seizures. All patients with altered mental status / seizure should have a point of care glucose, to ensure that is not the etiology. Intubation is indicated in this patient, as she is GCS 6 despite being 30 minutes post seizure (not protecting her airway). She also has a poor predicted clinical course as patients with TCA significant TCA overdose often get worse / die. Physostigmine is not a treatment for TCA overdose. It is a cholinesterase inhibitor.

stem: A 26-year-old female is brought to the Emergency Department (ED). She was at a football game and fell 20 feet from the stands. The paramedics have started two large bore intravenous lines and have placed her in a C-spine collar. Her vital signs on arrival to the ED: pulse 126/minute, blood pressure 76/40 mm Hg, oral temperature 37.2 degrees C, respiratory rate 22/minute, oxygen saturation on a non-rebreather mask 90%, point of care glucose -8.4 mmol/L. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally, the trachea is midline and there is no jugular venous distension. Heart sounds are normal. The pelvis is stable and there is no apparent femur fracture. She has an obvious open right lower leg fracture that has been splinted. Her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 8. What is the most likely source of shock?
answer: The correct answer is C. C; Shock in the setting of trauma should always be hemorrhagic until proven otherwise. You cannot have enough blood loss into your head to cause hemorrhagic shock. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage is less likely than intra-abdominal hemorrhage as the pelvis is stable. Pericardial tamponade and neurogenic shock are not forms of hemorrhagic shock and are far less common/likely than hemorrhagic shock. There are also no clinical signs to specifically suggest pericardial tamponade (e.g., muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension) or neurogenic shock (e.g., bradycardia, inappropriate vasodilation).

stem: Which of the following is the correct formula describing oxygen delivery?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 1). The lecture defines O2 delivery = cardiac output × arterial O2 content, and cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. O2 content is itself a sum: bound (SaO2 × Hb × 1.34, over 95%) + dissolved (PaO2 × 0.003, under 5%). E is the full product written out.

  • A, B: add flow to content instead of multiplying, so the units make no sense.
  • C: multiplies bound by dissolved O2; they should be added to give content.
  • D: subtracts dissolved from bound O2; dissolved oxygen adds to delivery.

stem: Which of the following statements is most correct?

options.html: The absence of a gag reflex suggests an inability to protect the airway
Abnormal vital signs always indicates the need for resuscitation
Chin lift is the initial maneuver of choice to open the airway in trauma patients
A venturi mask is a good initial choice in managing a patient with severe hypoxia
When assessing patients who are pulseless, you should not begin with the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) but instead address the circulation first

answer: The correct answer is E. E; Many normal people have an absent gag reflex at baseline. It should not be used as a method of assessing airway protection. Abnormal vital signs do not always indicate the need for resuscitation. When you are exercising your heart rate is high, yet you do not need resuscitation. Chin lift should not be used in trauma patients, as it involves head/neck manipulation which is contraindicated in the setting of potential c-spine injury. Jaw-thrust should be used instead. A venturi mask is not used in patients with severe hypoxia as it is not the highest flow FiO2 available. You should start high, then wean as tolerated. When assessing patients who are pulseless or unresponsive, you should start with a pulse check, so you address circulation first.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with a large area of redness and pain over his right thigh that developed over the past 48 hours. He has had a fever and feels generally unwell. He is alert and oriented. His vitals are as follows: BP 82/43 HR 135 RR 22 Temp 39.3ºC Oxygen saturation 95% on room air Does this patient have sepsis? Choose the best answer below:

options.html: Cannot determine until blood culture results are known
Cannot determine until lab results are back

answer: The correct answer is E. E; The clinical picture is consistent with a soft tissue infection. The qSOFA score for sepsis is positive for sepsis if at least 2 of the 3 clinical findings are present: 1) GCS < 15, 2), RR > or = to 22, 3) SBP < or = 100. This patient has 2 of these 3 criteria. Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis. You do not need to wait until blood cultures to come back (will take days, and are frequently negative even in presumed sepsis), or laboratory results. The SOFA score can also be used, and it does require the laboratory results to be back, but you can use the qSOFA score when laboratory results are not available.

stem: You are asked to assess a hypotensive adult patient. On examination vital signs are: HR 132, regular BP 86/48 RR 26 JVP low by clinical examination Periphery: warm with good capillary refill Temp 35.8ºC The most likely cause of shock in this patient is:
answer: The correct answer is E. E; While tachycardia, hypotension and tachypnea are clinical signs of many types of shock, the warm periphery with good capillary refill is the hallmark of distributive shock. Septic shock and neurogenic shock are both types of distributive shock. However, hypothermia (or hyperthermia) is typical of septic shock, not neurogenic shock. There is no such thing as "hypothermic shock".

stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted after a fall in the bathroom. Report from the paramedics is that he is unconscious with no response to voice, and flexion to pain on the left, extension to pain on the right. His right pupil is fixed and dilated. He is placed on a monitor; intravenous catheters are being inserted and blood work is being sent. He has noisy upper airway sounds that are improved with jaw thrust. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally, and trachea is midline. Heart sounds are normal. JVP is not visible above the sternal notch. Abdomen is slightly distended, with no guarding on examination. Vitals are: BP 104/68 HR 116 sinus RR 22 Temp 36.2ºC Oxygen saturation 85% on high flow oxygen non-rebreather mask The most appropriate next step in management is:

options.html: Emergency OR for presumed intracranial epidural hematoma

answer: The correct answer is C. C; While jaw thrust helped to open the airway, it is not protected (GCS<8) and predicted clinical course is poor (signs of brain herniation). Breathing is also concerning. Sats are poor even on high flow oxygen. This patient will also need to have a CT head, so will need to leave the monitored setting of the ED. Intubation is indicated for all of these reasons. It is not safe to have the patient leave the department without intubating first. A more detailed survey will also have to wait until ABCs have been addressed. Surgery will not be performed without imaging first to identify the type and location of bleeding. There is no current role for giving blood. While hemorrhagic shock from concomitant abdominal trauma cannot be excluded, Airway & Breathing still come before Circulation, and crystalloid would be given prior to blood.

stem: When dealing with a severely hypothermic patient, excessive mechanical jostling of a patient should be avoided because (of):

options.html: Increased regurgitation secondary to poor gastric motility
Susceptibility to hypothermia related orthopedic fractures
Hypothermic muscles are easily injured resulting in rhabdomyolysis
Increased shivering and oxygen consumption initiated by movement of the patient

answer: The correct answer is A. A; Excessive mechanical jostling should be avoided in severely hypothermic patients because it can precipitate serious cardiac dysrhythmias. The other listed answers are untrue.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is admitted with a history of three days of vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and distension. She is cold, clammy and has decreased capillary refill, and has had 12 ml of urine output over the last hour. Her vitals are: BP 120/86 HR 114 RR 18 Temperature 38.7ºC Is she in shock?

options.html: No, because her blood pressure is normal
Cannot say without knowing her response to intravenous fluid bolus
Yes, because she has evidence of decreased perfusion
No, because urine output is adequate

answer: The correct answer is D. D; Hypotension is not a requirement to make the diagnosis of shock. Patients with evidence of poor perfusion (cold, clammy skin, decreased refill, and reduced urine output), especially in the setting known volume loss, can be presumed to have shock.

stem: In late December, a community Emergency Department receives a warning call that paramedics will be arriving in 7 minutes with a 17-year-old female who was found VSA (Vital Signs Absent) and “cold as a rock” in the woods near her house. Her driver's license led police to contact her parents who last saw her 4 hours earlier. On arrival effective CPR is being carried out by paramedics. After aggressive rewarming and resuscitative efforts, the patient's temperature rises by 1.5°C. Her serum potassium level is 6.9 mmol/L (normal range 3.5-5.0 mmol/L). Her best chance for survival would be:

options.html: Bilateral chest tubes for thoracic lavage
Call nephrology to initiate STAT hemodialysis
Continue with current rewarming and resuscitation
Futile at this point. Efforts should be discontinued since neurologic outcome appears unfavourable
Transfer to a cardiopulmonary bypass or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation capable center

answer: The correct answer is E. E; Heated irrigation (thoracic lavage) is less effective than corporeal rewarming and associated with significant complications. The most effective form of corporeal rewarming is cardiopulmonary bypass or ECMO (better than hemodialysis). CPB or ECMO is the best choice for patients with hemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest or those who fail to rewarm with less invasive active internal rewarming techniques. Termination of the resuscitation would be inappropriate as the patient has not been adequately warmed, and potassium is not > 12. A very high potassium is a poor prognostic indicator and may be suggestive that resuscitation should be terminated.

stem: The American College of Surgeons have a classification of the stages of hemorrhagic shock. Which related statement is TRUE?

options.html: It can be used to accurately and reliably predict vital sign changes in patients with a massive intracranial hemorrhage
Urine output is a useful indicator of severity in the initial assessment of patients with hemorrhagic shock
Hypotension is an indicator of stage II shock
Pulse pressure is calculated by 1/3 x (SBP-DBP) + DBP
It does not accurately and reliably predict vital sign changes in all adult patients with hemorrhagic shock

answer: The correct answer is E. E; You cannot have enough blood loss into your head to cause hemorrhagic shock. Urine output is not a useful indicator of severity in the INITIAL assessment of patients with hemorrhagic shock, as urine output needs to be measured over the period of an hour or longer. Hypotension is an indicator of stage III shock, not stage II. Pulse pressure is calculated by SBP-DBP. While this classification system is useful, it does not accurately and reliably predict vital sign changes in all patients with hemorrhagic shock. Elderly patients, or those on medications such as beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, etc. may not have the same clinical signs at each stage of shock.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding methods of oxygen delivery?

options.html: 2L of oxygen via nasal prongs delivers an FiO2 of about 36%
A Venturi mask is an effective method for oxygen delivery in patients who are at risk for hypercarbia with uncontrolled oxygen therapy
A non-rebreather mask always delivers an FiO2 of at least 95%
A nebulizing / aerosol mask usually delivers an FiO2 of approximately 30%
Providing 8L of oxygen by nasal prongs is usually better tolerated by patients compared to using a face mask

answer: The correct answer is B. B; 2L of oxygen via nasal prongs only delivers an FiO2 of about 24%. A good guide: room air is 20-21%, then add about 4% for every 2 L via nasal prongs. A Venturi mask is an effective method for oxygen delivery in patients who are at risk of hypercarbia with uncontrolled oxygen delivery. It has an entrainment device that controls the FiO2. While a non-rebreather mask CAN deliver an FiO2 of up to 95%, it depends on the fit of the mask, and the oxygen flow rate from the tank. A nebulizing / aerosol mask usually delivers an FiO2 of about 40-60%. Providing 8L of oxygen by nasal prongs is usually not comfortable for the patients, as these high flow rates are very irritating to the nares.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the ED with a complaint of sore throat, difficulty breathing and feeling unwell for 48 hours. His GCS is 15 and he is able to speak full sentences, although his voice sounds abnormal. He looks moderately distressed, and you note audible stridor. He continually spits his oral secretions into a basin. His vital signs are as follows: HR - 122, BP - 148/92, RR - 28, T- 39.0°C, O2 sat - 98% Select the statement that is most TRUE with regards to his airway assessment.

options.html: His airway is patent as he is able to speak to you
His GCS is >8, so intubation is not indicated
His airway assessment demonstrates "problematic" features, and urgent expert assistance with airway management should be sought
His airway is patent as his oxygen saturation is normal
An oral airway should be placed immediately to manage airway obstruction

answer: The correct answer is C. C; Just because someone can speak to you, does not mean the airway is patent. He has evidence of abnormal patency with stridor, and muffled voice. Also, he cannot handle his own secretions, he has to spit them out continuously. This intubation should be assumed to be difficult and there is a need for urgent management, as the airway could completely obstruct at any moment. Getting help is prudent. Level of consciousness is not a concern, but that is only one indication for intubation. Airway patency is not assessed by oxygen saturation. That is part of your breathing assessment. If oxygenation is poor, it can be an indication for intubation.

stem: What is a clinical finding unique to distributive shock compared to other types of clinical shock?
answer: The correct answer is E. E; Distributive shock is the only type of shock that is associated with inappropriate vasodilation / normal capillary refill. Tachycardia, decreased urine output and altered mentation can be seen with any type of shock. Elevated JVP can be seen with obstructive or cardiogenic shock.

stem: A 35-year-old man collapses on arrival at the ED triage. You palpate his carotid artery and find that he is pulseless. You shout for help and for someone to go get the crash cart. Your next step should be:

options.html: Perform a head-tilt-chin-lift and deliver 2 rescue breaths
Start chest compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute
Place the man on his side in the recovery position

answer: The correct answer is B. B; In a pulseless patient, after calling for help, the next step is to start chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/minute. Once the crash cart arrives, a rhythm check can be performed and if the patient is in VF or pulseless VT, then defibrillation should be performed. There is no role for defibrillation if the rhythm is PEA or asystole. Cardioversion is reserved for treatment of rhythms with a pulse. Rescue breathing should be performed after the first 20 chest compressions. It is not the first step. Placing the patient in the recovery position is not an appropriate course of action in pulseless patients.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding accidental hypothermia?

options.html: A core body temperature of 29°C is classified as severe hypothermia
Providing warmed humidified oxygen is an example of active external rewarming
One risk of active external rewarming is core temperature after-drop
Hypothermia is defined by a core body temperature less than 36°C

answer: The correct answer is D. D; A core body temperature of less than 28 (not 29) degrees C is classified as severe hypothermia. Standard thermometers cannot measure below 34 C. Humidified oxygen is a method of active core rewarming, not active external rewarming. Hypothermia is defined by a core body temperature less than 35 C. One risk of active external rewarming is core temperature after-drop. Cold blood from the periphery returns to the core as extremities are rewarmed, and core temperature drops further.

stem: A 69-year-old woman is brought to the ED with a chief complaint of dyspnea. She has a witnessed VF cardiac arrest and after approximately 7 minutes of resuscitation, has return of spontaneous circulation. It is now 30 minutes post cessation of CPR, and she is still unresponsive. She has been intubated and has intravenous access. Which of the following are NOT priorities for her post-arrest care?

options.html: Ventilating at a rate of 14-16 breaths/min
Maintaining a MAP of >65 mm Hg

answer: The correct answer is A. A; Maintaining a MAP of > 65, obtaining an ECG, Targeted Temperature Management and glycemic control are all post-arrest care priorities. Ventilation at a rate of 10 breaths per minute is another target. You want to avoid hyperventilation, so a rate of 14-16 is too high.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding benzodiazepine toxicity?

options.html: All patients should receive flumazenil to help reverse toxicity
Oxygen should be provided to all patients with evidence of significant sedation
Mild hypotension is an unexpected complication
Combined ingestion with ethanol is more likely to require intubation
Tachycardia is a common vital sign abnormality

answer: The correct answer is D. D; Flumazenil should not be given to all patients with benzodiazepine toxicity because it can lower the seizure threshold. It is mostly reserved for use in iatrogenic toxicity, where it can be confirmed it is the sole toxin. Oxygen should not be provided to all patients with evidence of significant sedation. Only those with inadequate breathing/oxygenation. If given to all patients, it may lead to delayed recognition of respiratory deterioration. Mild hypotension and bradycardia (not tachycardia) are typical signs of benzodiazepine overdose. When benzodiazepines are combined with ethanol, there is substantial risk of respiratory depression, and need for intubation.

stem: All of the following are indications for a definitive airway EXCEPT:
answer: The correct answer is B. B; GCS < or = 8 is an indication for a definitive airway, not < 10. The others are all potential indications for intubation.

stem: A 21-year-old male falls 3 storeys at a construction site. As part of his resuscitation, he receives 15 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following complications would you NOT anticipate for this patient?

options.html: A platelet count of 102 x 109 (N 150-400 x 109)

answer: The correct answer is C. C; Packed cells are kept in a fridge, so rapid administration can lead to hypothermia. Massive transfusion of packed cells can cause coagulopathy from dilution of coagulation factors (high INR, low fibrinogen) and platelets (low platelet count). Hypocalcemia can occur with massive transfusion because the preservative citrate in packed cells binds calcium.

stem: A 42-year-old farmer presents to the ED after having a seizure. On examination you note that he has secretions that are frothing from his mouth, and tears draining from his eyes. His breathing is distressed, and auscultation of the chest reveals wheezes and harsh noises. The nurse comments that he has been incontinent of stool and urine. Which toxidrome has been demonstrated by this patient's presentation?
answer: The correct answer is E. E; This patient has symptoms compatible with cholinergic poisoning (salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, urination, stool incontinence and seizure). This is probably due to organophosphate poisoning, which is a pesticide

stem: When considering potential causes of a PEA cardiac arrest, which of the following are NOT part of the classic “H's” and “T's” that you should include in your differential?
answer: The correct answer is A. A; Hyponatremia is not one of the classic H's and Ts included in potential causes for PEA cardiac arrest.

stem: You are treating a 73-year-old female in the ED for pneumonia. Over the next few hours her systolic blood pressure gradually trends down below 100, and her oxygen requirements and work of breathing rise. When planning her resuscitation, which of the following do you NOT need to consider?

options.html: Which Personal Protective Equipment to don
The patient's advance directive regarding resuscitation
The patient's advance directive regarding organ donation
The Power of Attorney's direction regarding resuscitation

answer: The correct answer is D. D; When planning a potential resuscitation, you should consider which PPE to don, the patient's advance directive regarding resuscitation (if there is one), whether resuscitation would likely be futile, and the POA's directives regarding resuscitation (if there is a POA). While a patient may have an advance directive regarding organ donation, physicians do not decide whether or not to resuscitate a patient based on whether or not they are willing to be an organ donor.

stem: Which of the following are typical physiological adaptations to heat stress (acclimatization)?
answer: The correct answer is A. A; Increased plasma volume is a typical physiologic adaptation to heat stress. Others include decreased heart rate, decreased sweat sodium, increased sweat volume and earlier sweating onset.

stem: You are in the hospital cafeteria when you see a man collapse. CPR is started by a nurse near the man, and you run to get the crash cart, while another person calls switchboard to activate a Code Blue. When the monitor is attached, you determine that the patient is pulseless, and the rhythm displayed is attached. What is your best NEXT step?

options.html: Wait for the Code Blue team to arrive
Transport patient immediately to the ED

answer: The correct answer is D. D; The rhythm is VT. In a pulseless patient, when the defibrillator arrives, defibrillate immediately. Do not wait until the Code Blue team arrives. A synchronized shock is cardioversion, and is only used in patients with a pulse. Transporting the patient to the ED right now is inappropriate. You don't want to interrupt CPR or defibrillation to transport a patient in cardiac arrest. It could be considered later if needed.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ED via ambulance following a high-speed car crash. He is complaining of shortness of breath, chest pain and abdominal pain. His vitals are as follows: HR –142, BP –73/42, RR –32, O2 sat 82% on non-rebreather, T –37.0 oC EMS has placed the patient in a c-spine collar. The nurse has placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor. On examination you hear no stridor and voice is normal. There are diminished breath sounds on the right, and the trachea is deviated to the left. There is substantial bruising, crepitus and pain on palpation of the right hemithorax. His abdomen is diffusely tender. GCS is 14 and pupils are equal and reactive. a) What is your immediate management at this time (be specific)? You may list up to two. b) What additional area(s) of physical examination or adjunct(s) would you want in this patient (if any) as part your PRIMARY SURVEY? List up to 6.
answer: . a. This key feature question would be graded out of 1. The following would obtain 1 point: Needle decompression chest OR chest tube (1) The following would lead this to receive 0 points: Decompressing the LEFT chest Discharging the patient Sending patient outside of the ED for imaging Explanation: The clinical presentation is consistent with a right tension pneumothorax. This should be treated by decompression of the right thorax with needle and/or chest tube. Sending the patient home or sending for imaging outside of the ED is dangerous. b. b) This key feature question would be graded out of 6.0. The following would obtain 1 point each: Examine thighs / long bones / femurs (1) Look for external bleeding (1) Examine pelvis OR pelvis XR (1) Abdominal exam OR Abdominal PoCUS / FAST (1) CXR or POCUS chest (1) Group and screen OR crossmatch (1) The following responses would lead this question to receive a grade of 0: Listing advanced imaging like CT or MRI Sending the patient out of the ED / home Explanation: The primary survey involves a search for life or limb threatening injuries. These should include examination of the long bones, chest, pelvis, a search for external hemorrhage and PoCUS / FAST. It should not involve sending the patient for advanced imaging like CT or MRI, as they are too unstable to leave the ED. A CXR should also be done post chest tube insertion, but this part of the question is assessing for knowledge additional causes of shock in trauma besides the tension pneumothorax.

stem: 37. A 72-year-old female is found in bed in her apartment by her building manager after not being seen for 3 days during a heat wave in July. Her apartment has no air-conditioning. She has been brought to the ED by ambulance. Her vitals are as follows: HR –121, BP –85/48, RR –22, O2 sat - 96% on room air, T –42.0oC oral The nurse as placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor. She is confused (GCS = 13) and mucous membranes are dry. She denies any pain. Examination of the chest and abdomen are unremarkable. Her neck is supple and neurological examination reveals no focal findings. a) What is (are) your leading working diagnosis(es) at this time? You may list up to two. b) What is your immediate management at this time (be specific)? List as many as are appropriate.
answer: . a. This key feature question would be graded out 1 point. The following would allow the student to earn 1 point: Heat Stroke (1) Additional answers do not earn extra points. Explanation: Hyperthermia with altered mental status in the setting of heat exposure is likely heat stroke. There are alternative diagnoses, but this must be included in the top two. b. This question would be graded out of 4 points. The following would allow the student to earn 1 point each: Obtain IV access (1) IV crystalloid bolus (NS or Ringer’s lactate) (1) Start cooling (1) Obtain fingerpick glucose / point of care glucose (1) The following responses would lead this question to receive a grade of 0: Sending the patient for imaging outside of the ED Discharging the patient Explanation: This patient is in shock and needs rapid volume expansion with crystalloid. All patients with altered mental status should have a point of care glucose to exclude it as a contributing, reversible cause. Heat stroke should be treated with rapid initiation of cooling. Patients who are unstable should not be sent outside of the ED for imaging or discharged home.
